utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, sometime ago Judge Stephen asked whether the dots on the map represented the houses that were in a particular village and town. Regrettably, we are not able to answer your Honour's question precisely, but what we have done is obtain the legend of the map which indicates that they are houses and so forth and that may assist your Honour. I think the position is that as maps are upgraded, sometimes they put in the additional houses from the aerial photography or however they do it and sometimes they do not. That is why we cannot be precise about that. I tender this, your Honour. Might it be called P79A?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Prosecutor's 79?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 79 is the map and if that could be called 79A? Could you show it to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 79A will be admitted, Prosecution 79A. Mr. Tieger, were you questioning the witness, Mr. Arifagic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. MR. MESUD ARIFAGIC, recalled Examined by MR. TIEGER, continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the Exhibits which were before the witness when we adjourned can be replaced, 277A and 310, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, you are still under the oath that you took yesterday, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, before we adjourned yesterday, I believe you had described two occasions during which you saw Dule Tadic in Trnopolje camp. The second occasion was the one which you described when you were outside and he was with Goran Babic. Let me now ask you if you recall another occasion or the next occasion during which you saw Dule Tadic in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you at the time you saw him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was waiting to receive food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have two pictures, two photographs, of Trnopolje camp in front of you. Are you able to see the approximate location where you were at that time shown in either of those photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that the photograph of the school entrance shown front-on or the photograph with the logs in the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is of the photograph with the logs in it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May 277A be placed on the Elmo then? Mr. Arifagic, can you point out to us your approximate location on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was here. I was waiting here to receive food. Here were packages that people were distributing and we were standing lined up one by one here frontally like this, facing the asphalt which links to Trnopolje up to Kozarac. As I was receiving food, Dusan Tadic and Goran Babic in a car went on their way to Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you saw Dule Tadic he was in a car on the road which links Trnopolje to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was that car when you first saw it relative to your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The car was moving from the station towards Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as you were facing the road, then the car would be coming from your right side, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from my right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How fast or slow was the car going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I should say it was in a second gear. It was not moving fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was driving the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Babic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Dule Tadic sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the co-driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was in the passenger seat, in the front portion of the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of car it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A police car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As it approached in second gear from the direction of the station, did it then move past the position you were in and continue toward the direction of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this occasion was there another occasion on which you saw Dule Tadic in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excellent, very near I went past him and we looked one another into the face.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this occasion when you and Dule Tadic looked one another into the face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we wanted to leave Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the date that you left Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1st October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we place Exhibit 310 on the Elmo, please? Sir, on this photograph can you see the approximate location where Dule Tadic was when you saw him on October 1st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not approximately, but exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point out where that is, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That place is this one here. [The witness indicated on the photograph].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he on the inside of that fence or the outside of that fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was here, he put his hands like this on the fence and we were coming from there for the buses, so Dule was to my right and he was facing like that, and I was coming like that, and we looked each other into the eyes as we can look one another now, except that we were very close.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall about what time of day that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was about half past 8, since it was, it followed the alphabetical order and my surname begins with an A, so it was the morning, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you walked down this side walk and directly past Dule Tadic on your way to the bus which took you from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you walked by Dule Tadic, did you then board the bus that was to take you from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did that bus first go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As the buses were loaded one by one, we were setting off towards Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you being led by any Serbian authorities or camp officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know or recognise any of those persons who were leading the buses from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zdravko Torbica and Goran Babic. Goran Babic escorted us only up to Kozarac, and Zdravko Torbica continued on, that is, at the head of the column they went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they in any particular kinds of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of vehicles were they riding in or driving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Babic has, drives a police car. That is the same one he had in Kozarac. Zdravko Torbica drives an armoured vehicle, that is, a PAM which has never been in the police in Prijedor. Such a vehicle did not exist in Prijedor before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see Dule Tadic in court today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you point him out, please, and tell the Court what he is wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic is sitting down there between two policemen. He is nicely dressed, blue-ish suit, blue-ish shirt, a many coloured tie, clean shaven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is fine, sir, thank you. May the record reflect the identification of the accused, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Cross-examined by MR. KAY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, I would like to ask you questions first of all about how well you know Dusko Tadic. Were you a friend of his in that you socialised with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I knew Dule Tadic and I know him. I was not his close friend. You have two friends. You have house friends, family friends, and friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had not been to his house, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was only in front of their house, I remember well, as far as I know, when his father died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had not been in his house with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He had not been in your house with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You appear to have known friends of his that you knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You did not spend time in the evenings with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it was sometimes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often is "sometimes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not every night. I say sometimes, perhaps before 10 years or maybe before the war, or perhaps for two months, that we socialised, but I would be passing past his house every day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever drink in his cafe bar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which brothers of his did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule had three brothers. They were all older than he. Dule had Stojan, he had Mladen, he had Ljubo. Mladen is in Germany, Ljubo is in Banja Luka and Stojan married a Muslim ages ago, and there were some problems. I know that. Ostoja was saying, "Why is he marrying a Muslim?" but that does not really matter. That is all his family, and father best, as I have said, because we spent a lot of time at meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his brothers rather than Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His brothers were spending less time in Kozarac than Dule.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war in Kozarac, can you remember what Dusko Tadic looked like, say, at the beginning of 1992, three months before the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe him for us, what his appearance was then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please do so now for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a bit more weight then, and had a small beard, like they wear, and he was not shaven very often. It was not a big beard. It was just unshaven. Many wore it like that. It was ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was an appearance of not having shaved rather than wearing a beard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Goran Babic who you have told us that you saw Dusko Tadic with in Trnopolje on several occasions, were you aware of him being the police Commander in Kozarac at about the time you were in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that when I came from Omarska to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He previously worked with you in the police station before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the occasions you saw him in Trnopolje, was he acting or dressed as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What sorts of uniform would Goran Babic have worn as a policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Goran Babic was always an intelligent guy and skillful and as -- and he was always dressed in a blue police uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a plain blue police uniform or a blue camouflage uniform? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The police car that you saw Goran Babic in, was that the Kozarac police car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were such vehicles in Prijedor as well and in the police station in Kozarac. So whether this was a vehicle from Prijedor or Kozarac, I would not know, but they had the same and Omarska and Kozarac and Ljubija and Prijedor, because all the vehicles were being supplied by Prijedor, whether it was a Stojadin or not. But allow me to ask you something?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, sir, you cannot ask me questions, as her Honour will advise you. It is my job to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Only if you do not understand the question, then you can tell Mr. Kay, of course, that you do not understand the question and he will try to rephrase it. But, really, your responsibility is to respond to his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. [To the witness]: I would like now to turn to the first occasion that you say you saw Dusko Tadic in Trnopolje. Can you remember when it was, what the date was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could have been only after August 20th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you had been in the camp by then more than two weeks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You described him wearing camouflage uniform, multicoloured clothes, but what was the colour of that uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a military uniform, it is a green in there and like camouflage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, definitely not the police blue camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had been ill at this time and you were recovering after your experiences in Omarska which is why you were within the building, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you standing up when you were looking out of the window or were you lying down or sitting down? How were you positioned at the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time I was walking by the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were in Trnopolje camp itself at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That building where you were staying, did that have many people within it? Was it a crowded building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were naturally a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The position in relation to those guarding the camp at this time, were there many guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they stationed outside the camp or within the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards were around the perimeter, and who was looking for something, they would come inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the guards who were on duty at your camp? Did you recognise them because you were familiar with where they stood and what they did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you describe of seeing Dusko Tadic four times, it seems that you did not see him as a guard at the camp, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems from these four occasions that you saw Dusko Tadic, he does not seem to have been working as a guard at the camp, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the Commander of the camp whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero Curguz and, what do I know, those were the men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Slobodan Kuruzovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Kuruzovic, I also said, I was ill those 15 days when I came from Omarska, it forced me to walk, to watch, to see who there was, what there was, to find out where my family was, to find somebody to find that, and even though I could not, I was walking around more than I could, because when I came, whether my wife and children were there, and is there a friend to whom I could, whom I could address, and I said. So I just walked, and I did not have a desire to see anybody, and those who I knew I did not dare approach, but my only goal was to find out where they were. I have not come here to accuse anybody, to judge anybody. I just came here to say the truth, what happened. What I went through and what I know, and nothing -- as I said, nothing but the truth. That is why I am here, and because I walked around Trnopolje and moved around and it was by sheer accident that I saw. I was looking for help for my own family, just find out where my wife and my children were. I had a daughter of 17. I knew what was going on. I just wanted to know whether they were alive. I did not go around. I was not interested who was on guard, but I was interested because of my own family, if my family had been there I would not have been going around. That is what, so accident, that is -- sir, I respect you but I am just telling you why I did this, if you understood me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If we could look at that picture Exhibit 310 which is the school?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Your question was whether he knew about Kuruzovic. I do not know whether it has been responded to. Do you want to follow that up?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seemed to me in part but, your Honour, I will move on. That is a matter. [To the witness]: If we look at the photograph, Exhibit 310 -- have you got that before you -- which is the front part of the school? If it could be put on the monitor for you so that everyone can just see what we are looking at. You indicated to us yesterday where you were standing when you say you saw Dusko Tadic. It seemed that you saw him walking to the left of the picture between the trees that we see in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The window that you are looking from is a window in a part of the building that is set back from the two wings on the left-hand side and right-hand side, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say he was walking at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that he passed from, by my side, that is, maybe he did walk there, I do not know, but I saw him when he passed. You just look and you see and that is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you did not see him for very long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I did not even want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were looking out of that window, you did not communicate in any way to him, or you say you just observed the fact of him passing by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the distance from that window to the place where you say you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not paying attention to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were other people around you at the time in that part of the building when you looked out the window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I move on to the second time you say you saw him? This was on an occasion which was still within the scene of this photograph, you were sitting on the raised level to the right of the entrance in the middle of the school, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The area that Goran Babic and Dusko Tadic were in is further over to the left of this photograph, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where the logs were in the other photograph Exhibit, I think it is, 277?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again that is quite some distance away from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not measure it so I would not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time were other people around you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you indicate you saw them, it is towards the corner of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can now put that other photograph on the overhead projector? Thank you, Mr. Bos. Again it seems you were not observing the two people for very long?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for long.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because, as you said yesterday, you did not want to see them, so you left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did not dare ask them anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when this was, what date it was in terms of the length of your stay in Trnopolje, when it would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Date, no, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic at this time, can you remember how he was dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, again definitely not a blue camouflage uniform. It would have been a green camouflage uniform, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the camouflage, military, grey-ish uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is one which has predominantly an olive green colour within it, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again the third time you see him, that is with Goran Babic as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, I told you what my goal was. I was not going around the camp looking who was there. I just wanted to share with somebody where my family was. That is how I walked around. I observed, is there anybody whom I know who was a friend, to whom I could trust, even though I was ill then. That was my only goal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your stay in Trnopolje continued until October 1st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The only other occasion is on the day when you are leaving and he is by the fence of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he leaning against the fence? If we look at 310, that is the other photograph, if we can just put that on the screen? Where this photograph would have been taken is in the road, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This road goes in the direction, on the left-hand side towards the railway station, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the right-hand side up to Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he on the road side of the fence or on the other side of the fence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule stood here, that is, exactly by the fence watching who is passing by and going on to the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses were in the road at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not know at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were a large number of people at this time moving from Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems Goran Babic was with him again, but it was as a form of escort for the convoy that was moving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, up to Kozarac, as I said. Then he remained in the intersection of Kozarac. I was on the second bus and Babic stood by the road looking at Kozarac and we continued on towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It seems then that he was acting in his position as Commander of the police watching the convoy go, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger? Re-Examined by MR. TIEGER

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think just one question, your Honour. Mr. Arifagic, after your bus was loaded with the prisoners, did it leave the area of Trnopolje camp and go in the direction of Kozarac, then wait for other buses to be loaded and then joined your bus before the whole convoy left for Prijedor and ultimately Karlovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is all, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour. Examined by the Court

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Witness, I wonder if you can tell me something about how you got food at Trnopolje. There were no regular meals supplied week after week. How did you get food there -- not only you but the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food, until the Red Cross started issuing packets, that was better, but before then, until they started distributing, I do not know what I found to eat. When we arrived to Trnopolj from Omarska and people got out of the camp when they were going for food, some of them would not come back. Then we did not even go to look for food.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But during all those weeks you were there, you must have had some need for food. How did you get it? Where did it come from, if it was not supplied by the camp authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said, the Red Cross was distributing packets. That one packet was good for 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was all through the time you were in Trnopolje there were Red Cross parcels?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was for me upstairs. Downstairs, who were healthier, who were down by the older, they had a cold room or something, but those were lines who were able to stand for three, four hours and maybe they got some of that water, I do not know. I do not know what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger? Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Mr. Arifagic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Arifagic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much for inviting me to say the truth and nothing but the truth and, I said already, I did not come here to accuse or to judge, only to tell the truth, what happened, what I went through and what I know, and thank you very much for inviting me. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I call Bahrija Denic. MR. BAHRIJA DENIC called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Denic, would you please take that oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Solemn declaration. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you sir. You may be seated. Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bahrija Denic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1st June '54.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what part of the town of Kozarac did you live for most of the time you were there up until the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said, I was born in '54. I lived in the lower part of the town towards Trnopolje, the place, the locality is called Suhi Brod. In '68 we moved towards Kozarac, that is, some 500 or 600 metres towards Kozarac, from the centre about one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked first for a construction company, Put, Sarajevo. Then I went to Slovenia. From 1980 I worked in Croatia for Sava Sunja company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work for this company up until 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return back to Kozarac on a regular basis when you were working in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, did you maintain your family home in Kozarac all during this period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a house, my wife, my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They all lived in Kozarac when you were working in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service from 1973 to '74 in Serbia, in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your ethnic group Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you work up until the war in Croatia started in 1991 and from that time onwards were you sent home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you came back to Kozarac did you work in that period from the end of 1991 through to May 1992 with a telephone company in the Kozarac area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Kozarac when it was attacked on 24th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and your family proceed to a nearby village called Softic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then did you return back to your home on 26th May in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay there until the voluntary surrender of the people of Kozarac on 27th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was some two kilometres away from my home, and later on a group of us, of some 150 to 180 persons, had to surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it, what place did you surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We surrendered in Kozarac at the intersection Kozarac/Trnopolje/Prijedor/Banja Luka. Next to the petrol station there is a bus stop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you surrender to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We surrendered to the army, the police, and there were all sorts of colours, insignia, clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a combination of the military and the police, the people that were there when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were they doing with the people when you surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we surrendered they ordered us to separate men from women, and men below -- males below the age of 16. I and other men moved to one side, and women and children went to the other. We waited there for one hour, perhaps a little more, until buses arrived and we were ordered to board them. As I was boarding, I asked one, he was a policeman, "If we are not going together, women and men, may I take my father to the women, since my father was of a very advanced age", and they allowed me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, the women and your father and others were separated from yourself and were you then placed on a bus with the other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the buses then go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The buses headed for Prijedor and we had reached the Keraterm factory, and we stayed there on the buses until other buses formed to move on, and where we were to go, I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at Keraterm, did you get out of the buses or did you stay on the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We stayed on the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay there for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be two hours, perhaps a little longer, but around two hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that then did the buses move off again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that the buses went through Prijedor and through Tomasica to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in the Omarska camp, were you detained in the cafeteria building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was, I and many other inhabitants of Kozarac, we were told to enter a room, a place which was in that building as part of the cafeteria, and there we spent from Wednesday evening until Friday some time in the afternoon, and after I was interrogated I was transferred to another room which was above the dump truck garage. I went up some stairs and I and other people who had been interrogated were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the Omarska camp were you beaten or otherwise mistreated yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every day when we went to eat, there were blows, they were hurrying us up, "Eat as fast as you can, enter as fast you can, go out as fast as you can". As we would walk back to our rooms, we would be beaten with the rifle butts, with batons, with all sorts of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from these beatings which were singled out to most of the prisoners as they attended their meals and so forth, were you ever specifically beaten or abused on any one particular occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in Omarska, they did at Manjaca. In Omarska they took others out, ill-treated them, beat them. People died because of severe injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know anyone in the Omarska camp who was taken from the camp and who has not been seen since?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew for certain, if I had a list now, but I can vouch that I knew 100 or, perhaps, 200 individuals who were taken out and are still missing. We have heard stories that they had been exchanged, that they were swapped in Bihac, but there is no information and there are my relatives, my family, my neighbours among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave the Omarska camp? What date was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the Omarska camp we went on 6th or 7th of August and on the 1st August my brother died in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got on to the buses, a camouflage soldier told us to look the other way from the driver, so that we could not really orient myself where they were taking us, but throughout the time we had to sing, and they beat those first ones. We saw their injuries later on, and later on we learned that we had arrived in Manjaca. But before that in Han Kola, our buses were stopped and they showed us to the locals saying, "Here come the Turks. Now is your opportunity to take your vengeance".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anything happen to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I and my son were taken out from the bus at Manjaca and beat me on one side of the bus and my son on the other. How long it took, I do not know. I only know that at some point they ordered us to go back into the buses. I did not really think about myself so much. I was trying to hear what they were doing to my child and how he behaved. When I saw that he was alive I felt better immediately. Although later, for five or six days, I was lying down in those stables, in that barn, where they kept us and I survived even that. They did not kill me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any one guard ever attack you with a knife when you arrived at the Manjaca camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was attacked and cut my back and carved a cross at Manjaca. That was that same evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you still have the scar from that cross that was cut into you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. It is still visible a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the camp at Manjaca for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed until the 23rd August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that we were called out up there at Manjaca and did not tell us where we were going. As we were going by in groups of five holding hands, I saw also there was a group of men next to the road with their backs on us. We got there and they loaded us on to the buses and we set off. When we arrived in Kozarac, I saw as we went past Omarska to Kozarac, and then I was only looking whether it would turn off to Trnopolje or go on to Prijedor. They turned towards Trnopolje and then I realised we were going to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you arrived at Trnopolje camp, where were you placed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Trnopolje, when I arrived there, I spent the night first in a hall, in the old centre, and then the next day when I came out of there, they allowed me to wash myself. Some relatives gave me some little food to eat and then I moved to the new school upstairs to a room next to the gymnasium, and I was there until we went to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the relatives had got the food from that they gave you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My relatives, the food they got, I cannot tell you exactly, but I guess they managed to get some food, whoever managed to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 1st September.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that period were you given food at the camp by the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get food? What did you do for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the beginning food was brought by a van, I do not know who it was, and that we who had come from Manjaca, some said there, "Well first we must feed you a little bit and then you will go", but that was very little. It would not fill a tooth. Then I went out to the first houses where there were quince trees and I would make a kind of tea and that is what I ate and drank.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you went out and picked fruit off the trees to supplement your diet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was still fruit when I arrived from Manjaca. There was a quince tree. After that, an international organisation came and registered all those people in the camp, and then they started giving us out those packages, parcels and things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in Trnopolje camp did you ever see men taken out in groups to, allegedly, perform work duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it with my own eyes because I arrived from Manjaca at a later stage. Once I did see an incident when one Cavic was looking for someone to go buy plums for him, and people avoided it and I did not go to work anywhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why people were avoiding this, avoiding being taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because it was dangerous, because one called Hase went out and did not come back, he and two more, and probably it happened before my time, so people must have known that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, I have known him for some 20 years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know him from the time when you went to school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, except that he was younger, so he was in a lower grade than I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you lived in the town of Kozarac did you see him from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I would go to Kozarac, to the centre, to the marketplace, I would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where the Tadic family lived in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I know where his father had a house and I know where he had a house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what Dule Tadic did in Kozarac immediately prior to the war for a living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he had his restaurant and I presume that is what he made his living on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know his parents, his mother and father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I knew his father and mother too, but not as -- well, I could not say that I knew her as my neighbours, neighbours with whom we visited, but everybody knew them in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether or not Dule Tadic was interested in sport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what type of sport, in particular?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you see Tadic prior to the war, the commencement of the war, in Kozarac in May '92, the last time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last time it was on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is the Thursday before the Sunday attack, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you see him on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We met in the street, on the road leading to Kozarac from intersection Prijedor/Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you met, did you actually meet with him or did you just see him on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we just walked past one another. He was walking down one side of the road and I was on the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you acknowledge him or speak to him or did you just observe him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not talk. I nodded in greeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall whether on that occasion he was dressed in civilian clothes or in a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the next time after that occasion that you saw Dule Tadic, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him when I was coming out from the camp at Trnopolje and as I was boarding the buses going to Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the date, what was the date when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the 1st October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About what time of the day did you see him? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it could have been sometime around midday, around noon, when we were boarding buses. As we were boarding them in groups, there were very many buses, and they requested strict discipline when boarding buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was Dule Tadic when you saw him on this occasion when you were boarding the buses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was boarding the bus, he was standing to the left, perhaps four, six, seven metres away, on the left-hand side next to the fence of the school, he was standing there, he and two more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall how he was dressed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in a sort of a police uniform, grey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any head wear that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you see whether or not he was armed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could not see that, because as you were called out you had to go out and board the bus, so that one could not really look around that much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he see you, do you think, when you were coming out to board the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I cannot say, maybe yes, maybe no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Denic, I am going to ask you, if you would, please, to look around the courtroom and tell me if you see the person you know and recognise as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do. That is him over there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please tell us how he is dressed and where he is located in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is located to the left between two policemen. He has a blue suit, a blue shirt, a tie.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might the record reflect, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, do you have cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one question, your Honour. Cross-examined by MR. KAY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The uniform that you recollect Dusko Tadic wearing on 1st October when you were boarding the buses to go to Karlovac at Trnopolje, was that basically the colour blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not blue, strictly speaking. It was like the police used to wear in the then Yugoslavia, approximately that colour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that have blue in the colours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not blue, blue. It is a -- there is a brown-ish blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will not ask a third question. I asked two. That is all I ask. Examined by the Court

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Denic, was it a camouflage uniform or was it a solid ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not camouflage, not a camouflage, like the policemen used to wear before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A solid colour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One colour, yes, yes, yes, one colour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, I have nothing further in re-examination, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay? Further cross-examined by MR. KAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I just have one question now following on. [To the witness]: Was it the winter police uniform, a serge blue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, because it was still a warm month.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Denic being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Denic, you are permanently excused. You are free to leave. Thank you for coming. We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. (11.30 a.m.) (Short adjournment) (11.50 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, just before I call the next witness, witness No. 72 on the list indicated to me this morning that he would like limited protective measures, namely, that his face be distorted on the television screen and that he be assigned a pseudonym. Other than that, he would just give his evidence in open court. I think I have the latest list, your Honours. The one I am reading from is 7th August 1996. It is No. 72. I have discussed this with the Defence, your Honours. We will file a motion at lunch time, but of course he is expected to be the witness after the next witness that I am about to call. What I think we will do is change the order around and call 73 ahead of 72, that is, Samir Hodzic we will call after the next witness. I should indicate at this stage that we are not calling witness 71 as it appears on the list.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 72 will be the next one after the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But you are omitting 71?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: 71 is being omitted. I should say at this stage 74 is not going to be called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 74 will not be called?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour. So the order will be 70, 73 and 72. We will file the motion at lunch-time in relation to 72.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to the request regarding witness No. 72 on the witness list, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann has been good enough to explain it to me this morning. Of course, the testimony of the witness will still be able to be heard and so it is merely a question of image to which we do not object.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And the pseudonym, no objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The request will be granted. If we receive the motion in time, we will enter a written order before the witness; if not, we will proceed with the witness's face distortion and pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If it please your Honour. Your Honour, there is another matter. I tender, pursuant to the provisions of Rule 70 of the Rules, documents in relation to the camp at Trnopolje. We have also made copies of these, one each for your Honours. They are not the colour copies. They are black and white copies. We will endeavour to obtain colour copies and substitute them at a later stage. If I might tender those, your Honour? The original is the colour copy.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What subsection of Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It is (C), your Honour, subsection (C).

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: This is in connection with the next witness we will be hearing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will show it to the next witness, your Honours. My understanding of Rule 70 is it seems you do not necessarily tender it through a witness is the way it seems to operate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Does it relate to this next witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The next witness will be shown the Exhibits, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think, for ease of reference, your Honours, it is probably better if we refer to it as Exhibit 311A, B and C; A being the map of 2nd August 1992, B being 13th August 1992 and C being 7th September 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there an objection from the Defence? Mr. Orie?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: We have just got copies from the Prosecution, your Honour, and we have some difficulties with these documents as to their accuracy. So I do not know how to deal with that, but if we are under Rule 70(C), and if we are not convinced that these are accurate documents, then the Court "may not order either party to produce additional evidence received from the person". I do not know exactly what the consequences are. I would like to discuss it first before we finally -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I believe we have received another exhibit, you did not designate it though, being offered under 70(C), but did we not receive another exhibit signed by the same person who is indicated on this letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If you are going to question the witness, let us see where we are. At that point we can admit it provisionally, subject to your challenging its authenticity. Is that what you wish to ascertain?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: If this is shown to any witness and if any questions are put to him on this material when it is not inaccurate in our view, of course, we would like to know where it comes from and how it has been created, etc. etc. We have not been able to analyse it properly. We have only had a glance at it and we found some inconsistencies with our photographic material we made at the spot.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: As I understand the Prosecutor, he will discuss this Exhibit with the witness, but of course this witness will not be able to vouch for its authenticity. So, if you need time to verify its authenticity, maybe we can just admit it provisionally, subject to a challenge that you may have at a later time and, depending upon that challenge and how we will rule on that challenge, then strike the testimony and the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I think that would be a good solution because we do not know whether the inaccuracies are relevant or not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. We will handle it that way. Would you call your next witness, please, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, the Prosecution calls Eniz Besic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Then 311A, B and C will be admitted, subject to that challenge, Mr. Orie. MR. ENIZ BESIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that has been given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MR. NIEMANN

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, what is your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Eniz Besic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born 22nd October -- November [sorry] 1946.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Kozarac, that is, in Besici, one kilometre from the centre of Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend your primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your secondary school in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you live for the most part of your life leading up to the war in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spent all my life on my property, in my house, in Besici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Besici? In what direction is Besici from the centre of the town of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is towards Mrakovica, the left hill, that means the north, north of Kozarac, one kilometre adjoining a settlement so that it stops about 1.5 kilometres. So from Kozarac towards Mrakovica, that would be on the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your occupation up until the commencement of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a professional driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you drive a vehicle at the Ljubija mine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I drove a truck which supplied food for the kitchen and such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do your military service from 1966 to '67?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do that in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a Bosniak of Islamic faith.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you keep working for up until the commencement of the war, how long before the commencement of the war did you continue to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand the question. How long did I work for the company and up until when, prior to the war? Could you please repeat the question? How much in terms of years of service that I had or when did I stop before the war started?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you stop before the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped working a week before the outbreak of the war, because the Serbs put up their check points on the road between Kozarac and Prijedor and they were checking all the IDs, all Muslims. Then one day they turned back all the Muslims and they had no opportunity to go to work and then I was turned back too. I called, the phones were still working, so that I called my boss and I told him that I could not come to work and he replied, "Stay home and I will treat you as if you were on vacation".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Kozarac when it was attacked on 24th May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately, what time of the day was it when the attack started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was, I believe, about 1 o'clock in the afternoon, 1.00, 1.20, around 1 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you initially seek shelter in the basement of your house during the course of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with my family and some neighbours. We all took shelter because the shelling had started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then later did you go into the forest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after we saw that the Muslim villages were starting to go, they started to burn one by one, and we got information that Chetniks started slaughtering everyone, myself and all my neighbours went to the forest to look to save ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some days later, on 27th May, did you surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we also had information that it would be good that we surrendered because they started to shell the forest as well where the civilians are. There were some casualties there so we did not know where to go, at home or at the forest, and all that was remained -- had remained was to collect women and children and to go to the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you surrendered did you have with you a white flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to in order to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started down our village, down our road, towards Kozarac, to the centre, where other columns from other directions were joining in there. So that at a bridge called Mutnik where the warehouse was, we had our first encounter with Chetniks, that is, the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Serb soldiers then start to walk beside the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they started to walk. Before the meeting point, before the bridge across the river, I saw a trailer, a tractor, which was parked which was covered with blankets. Myself and my neighbour came over. It was with another tractor. It was sitting on the road and there were a lot of dead bodies, corpses. There were female corpses. A day before, a shell hit the column and then they loaded them up, so that I could see with my own eyes that trailer, I do not know how many, but there were five, six, seven. They were loaded up like logs. There were a number of women there. That was my first encounter with casualties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to with this column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went with the column to Prijedor. They separated us. Women and children were travelling on the left side of the road, the highway Banja Luka/Prijedor, and men went on the right-hand side towards Prijedor, and that is how the column was moving. But they were shooting as if somebody was attacking us, but that was only to intimidate us, obviously, the civilians, men and children and women. So they would order us, command us, and we would have to lie down. The first bus stop was called Limenka. We had to lie down in the field, in the ditch, and then I had bad luck to lie down next to a corpse. It was a civilian. Somebody recognised him, who it was, and I know who it was but I do not want -- I would not like to mention his name. Perhaps his family is still hoping that he is alive but, unfortunately, he was lying dead in that ditch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The translation of your answer starts: "We went with the column to Prijedor". Is it correct that you went in the direction of Prijedor? You did not walk all the way to Prijedor from Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For about how far did you walk towards Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was called Ziko's restaurant. That was also a bus stop. Since I am a driver, I think it was four to five kilometres, the distance, between Kozarac and what we walked -- the distance that we walked. There the buses started arriving, and they were loading, first, women and children and then we -- then the men came and we were put on the buses and taken to Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you were put upon the buses, were the Serb soldiers searching people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, twice. The search was first when they were separating us from our spouses and our children. That was the first search. Then the second search was when we were boarding buses. Everybody had to spread their arms and somebody would get hit. They would curse Alija or mother or something, and they took everything out, even the nail clippers were not left. They took my wallet, money. Then I asked him to give me back my documents, personal documents, my driver's licence. I recognised a colleague, another driver, a Serb, and he -- I asked him whether we could go back because I knew where my wallet was thrown away by a Serb soldier. I told him I did not care about the money, but I wanted the documents at least, because I may need them, that I could say who I was and that I was not guilty. He laughed to that and he said, "You will not need them, you will not need documents". That was a bit unclear to me and then it was clear as if it had been planned that we would be liquidated, if I did not need documents, I do not know why else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go in the bus?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started going towards Prijedor in buses to the so-called Cirkin Polje which is a suburb of Prijedor. Then they turned left towards the silo. Since I knew all those roads, I knew where we were going. Then they turned to the then old road which was going towards Trnopolje which, sort of, followed the railroad tracks, but we had no opportunity to watch, because we had to have our heads bowed with our hands on top of the -- but I could, sort of, I had a sense of where we were going because I knew all those places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the bus subsequently arrive at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it arrived and they ordered us to get off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got off the bus at the camp, approximately what time of the day was this, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was already -- it was past, it was at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The day was 27th May 1992, the same as day as you surrendered, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, I remember that date. It was a Wednesday, 27th May, when we disembarked. I saw a lot of people, a lot of civilians. When we got off the bus, then they started spraying rounds of bullets and I think it was also a form of intimidation so we had to lie down. They said that ours were shooting. I do not know who the "ours" were. We were civilians. We had no weapons. Then they started cursing and they said, "It is yours that are shooting. Lie down". So there were tractors, there were trailers. Then we lain underneath until they ordered us to get back up, like the danger was over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the camp were you then reunited with your family?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there by accident I found my spouse and my younger son who was then 15 years of age. He was lucky to have left with his mother, my wife, and we all were reunited there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to stay together or were you separated again from your wife and younger son?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They separated us again, so that my wife and some other women and children were taken outside of the camp to the houses that they said were also a part of the camp and were under their control. So that it would be better for them to be there than to be with all -- with this crowd of people there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Myself, the first two or maybe three nights, I do not know, I remained and I slept under a truck, under a tractor. We had to make do, as best we could, under the trailers, the tractor. Then we found a spot in the cinema theatre, that was the old dom, because we figured that it was safer than outside. There was a lot of shooting and the bullets were flying into the trailer under which we were sleeping, but then we got inside and it was full, there were a lot of small children, babies. They were crying all night long, so that that too was terrible, but a bit safer than outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have your two elder sons with you during this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both my sons. We never separated. Wherever I went, they did. I found them some crates, some plastic beer and juice crates and they were lying on those crates and I was lying on the concrete, so I arranged that for them. There was a Coca-Cola crate. It was a bit more comfortable. That is where they slept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately, how many people can you estimate were at the camp when you arrived on 27th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All total within the camp, there were a lot of people. Later, when we were the fewest remained, when we were registered by the International Red Cross, we were of 1600. That was the low number, but when we first arrived there were several thousands, maybe 3,000 or 4,000 in the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp, was it set up as a camp? I mean, were there fences around it? Were there guards, checkpoints? Can you describe how it was organised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were guards. There were checkpoints. There were no fences. There were no wires at first, but there were guards. There was military. There was a lot of shooting, that was intimidation, and the fence was put up later. They were putting it up, taking it down. But at first it was beehive, everything, there were men and women and elderly men and all ages. They were all there. Sick were coming too. They were carrying them in wheelbarrows, the immobile people, really old. So, at the beginning it was pretty unorganised. What they did, they were patrolling around the road and they were shooting, intimidating, so that the people would not flee. They were also calling people out. They were looking for people. There were lists that were made. That was in the first days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The guards at the camp, do you know whether they were attached to the military or the police or was it some other organisation, did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were regular soldiers of theirs, some reserve soldiers. There were also police when there was something, some curfew or they were bringing somebody, then they brought reinforcements, then they would have military and civilian police arriving. If there would be a normal day without, how should I put it, something more interesting in terms of comings and goings, then there were the regular Serbian Army, dressed in their regular uniforms and those were present the most and they were keeping guard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your time in the Trnopolje camp, were you interrogated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times I went to interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first time you were interrogated, where did they conduct the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first time I happened to be outside there was a civilian inmate taking along a Serb soldier. This Serb soldier had a sheet of paper with my name on it, and then my brothers and my one of my nephews, so I saw a few names written on it. This neighbour of mine, he pointed with his finger at me and said, "This is that Besic".
