He told me, "Would you come with me?" and I said, "Yes" because I saw that he was carrying a rifle and, as we were moving among the civilians, among the inmates, we moved towards the centre, towards this hall, and he asked me ,"Where is your rifle?" and swore at my mother and said, "Where is your rifle? Where did you hide it?" I said I had never had a rifle. He took me to his Commander, to a room. This was formerly the office of the Local Commune, or something. It was quite small but it was a part of that cinema.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it something referred to as the dom building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is all within the confines of the dom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were interrogated were you beaten or mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, first, I had to write a statement where I had been, what I had been doing, if I had any weapons, which one of my neighbours were in possession of arms, what political party I belonged to and things like that, and I had to write that down and then read it. What I wrote down, I then read. If they were not satisfied with it, then a beating would ensue. They had special instruments for beating, and they were very poor experts in beating with police batons. When they would beat me with police batons, I could somehow endure it, rather, simply I could bear it. It did not hurt that much. But when they beat me with wooden instruments, they would make sticks of wood, and those were blows, very hard and very painful. With these they beat me, three of them, and then they would have enough and when they would have enough, they would again put me up on the chair and make me continue writing my statement. So that I had to write whatever they ordered me, what was true and what was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the names of any of the people that beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Their Commander was Slavko Puhalic because they turned to him and he was quite civil with me. He said, "You interrogate this guy. Let him make a statement and be free", and then he went out into the field to find a rifle or some inmate or something. But three of them stayed behind, just soldiers, privates. They were not policemen, just ordinary soldiers. I used to know one from before, not much but I knew him. His name was Mladen Mitrovic. The second one was, sort of, a round cheeked, rather small. He was Zeljko Rudak. The third one I did not know. He had chestnut hair. He was clean shaven. But they all treated me equally, more or less. Then followed beatings and there was also music. They had a transistor radio or a cassette. The music, they played it very loud. It seemed easier to beat alongside the music also so that my screams and the cries of pain of other inmates would not be heard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the person was Zeljko Rudak, is it, the guard who beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of these beatings, did you suffer some broken ribs and did you suffer internal kidney damage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but before they started beating me, they beat one Demirovic called "Began", and I was standing in the corner of this room and he was severely beaten and I watched that. When they finished with him, they told me, "Did you see what happened to him?" I said, "Yes". "So if you do not tell the truth, you will fare even worse". That is how it was. I told the truth, but I fared as bad as he or, perhaps, even worse. Yes, I did suffer the effects of the beatings, of the blows on the head, because I had to beat my head against the floor. They said, "Now beat your head, since it is foolish, since it voted for the SDA", and they also hit me with their boots in the kidneys, and I lost my consciousness several times. I was in a coma. They would, sort of, arouse me, sprinkle some water on me and then put me up again in the chair to go on writing. I had to write what I was ordered to. If I did not write what they said, then beatings would follow. If I would write down what they told me to, I would have to read it out and then they would laugh and look at each other and say, "Look at what he wrote", and then they would swear at my mother, and they made it precise, the "balija" mother, and "write". So if I wrote, I would be beaten. If I did not write, I would be beaten the same. Then, when some three hours had gone by, I was already quite deadened and I really wished they would kill me, they would finish me off with a bullet. Then Mladen Mitrovic took out a knife and put it at my throat and asked me, "Do you know this knife?" "No", I said. He said, "That is your knife". I said, "No, it is not my knife", I said, "nor has it ever been". "Yes, yes", he said. "You have cut the throats of many Chetniks with this knife". I said, "No, I hate slaughtering chicken, let alone men". He said, "Well, if you did not, even if you did not, now you will be slaughtered with it", and then with their blows, under the blows I fell down again on the floor and he knelt on me to cut my throat, but he did not turn the edge of the knife. He turned the blunt side of the knife and pressed it against my throat. I expect -- and I thought that that was the end of me then. But he was only trying to scare me and he pressed again with the blunt edge of the knife against my throat and then he changed his mind. He said, "Well, we will not kill you now". So, as I could not stand up myself, they put me on my feet and put me against the wall. So ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mladen Mitrovic then cut you with a knife on your chest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then when they put me up so as not to slaughter me, then on my chest he cut a cross, he said, "As of today, by today is Bajram . Bajram is a Muslim holiday and on your Bajram you will become a Serb for all times", and that is when he carved a cross in my chest and hit me with his knife in the chest and said, "As of today you are a Serb. Throughout your life you will be a Serb". So I still have a scar and I still have kidney complaints, and I have other pain and I still have pain, chest pain, because of all those blows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to cutting a cross on to your chest, did he force you to make the religious sign of the cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to make a sign of a cross, that Serb sign. I do not really know. I did not choose my religion. I did not choose my parents, who will sire me. It was by chance that I was born a Muslim, but he forced me to make a sign of a cross with my hand, but I did not know that Catholics made a different sign of a cross from the Orthodox. So, unfortunately, I chose so to cross myself as a Catholic and they also hate Catholics as much as they hate Muslims, so then he said and hit me, "Look at this Ustashe, fuck his mother. He is making an Ustashe sign of cross". So I had to repeat that under the blows from all three of them until I learnt the sequence of making that sign of a cross, that sequence, and they would get confused and, unwittingly, they would hit one another. So that one of them would say, "Oh, ouch, you have hit me", and then they would go on beating me until I would fall down on the floor under the blows, and sometimes I even had to pretend I had fainted so they would stop for a while and I could rally a little bit. On a number of occasions I fainted truly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About two weeks later did you go for a second interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they again called out "Besic", those namesakes of mine, so that the turn of my two sons also came. They entered first for interrogation and another neighbour whose name is also Besic, and I was waiting outside. A Serb was walking up and down outside and asking from a policeman who had lined us up and was standing beside us to finish us off, go quickly, that is, to shoot us. This one just indicated him with his head to get lost. But he persisted, "Let me settle the accounts with them. I will do it quickly", and that was very disagreeable, whether this policeman would yield or not. But the policeman was insistent and he managed to chase that guard from us. Then I was also driven into the room where my sons were and the sons were taken out into another room, and I entered to the interrogator. The interrogator seemed slightly to be taken unawares. So he asked me, "How are you? What are you? What are you doing here", and such like and said, "Well, you are a good fellow, what are you doing here in the camp?" I said, "I have not the slightest, everybody is here and so am I". "So what is new", he said, "what do I know? What do I know about politics?" and so, and I told him, "Well, you know that I was doing my job, that I am a driver, not a politician. I am not interested in that, that I had friends, Serbs and Croats, and all religions, I mean". He said, "Yes, I know, you are a good chap, but you see those three who are interrogated before you, they have been picked out for liquidation". He had in front of him a sheet of paper. There was a list, a complete list, of us due for interrogation. In the right-hand corner of that sheet of paper it was noted in red pencil, and I saw it was my two names and my neighbour Teofil Besic who were picked out for finishing off, and that went liquidation to Omarska. I said, "Well, these are my sons." He was surprised and said: "Oh, fuck your God, I could have killed your sons." I said like this: "Well, if you can spare my children."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, he said: "Well, since you are a good chap, here, I will save your children." At that moment another Serb came in, a guard, and he hugged this interrogator. The interrogator, he was an army officer, I knew him but I did not know his name, he knew me better, he sort of said: "I am your friend", and I did not know, but I was perhaps lost. I could not remember his name. I still do not know who he is. I do not know who interrogated me. I know him by sight but I do not know his name. Another guard entered and hugged him, so they enquired after each other's health. Then he turned his head towards me, because I was sitting next to him, and he said: "Who's that?" He said: "That's a friend of mine." Then this one, that Serb who came in, asked: "Where do you work?" I said that I worked at the mine, I was a driver. "Oh" and then he swore at my mother: "You compiled lists, so that we ought to liquidate all Serbs, all guards", that is that the Muslims were making lists to liquidate Serbs. I said: "I did not make any lists nor do I know of any such lists." Then a blow ensued, a very strong one. I do not know if he had anything in his hand or not, but I almost fainted. Then he started for his pistol, but the one who interrogated me first, he jumped up and separated us and said: "Get out, get lost and take your children to the school", and that is how it was. That is how this interrogation ended without a major tragedy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from these two integrations, were you ever singled out again for interrogation during the period of time that you were in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was yet another time when I was singled out, but it was not that. Then I was only hit once with that police baton, with a truncheon, and he hit me only once, but that was in passing only. So the third time I was not really beaten as the first time. The first time was quite enough. I was immobile for 15 days. My sons took me to the toilet and when I needed to turn over they had to do it. One would take me by the shoulders and one by my feet and they would turn me to the other side. I could lie only sideways. I could not lie on my back or on my chest because my chest was badly injured and bloody. People would come to see me and those who would see me would turn their heads away from me and would not ever want to see me again, but I survived that. It was ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were at the camp were many of the prisoners taken away for interrogation that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many were interrogated there, but many were also taken to Keraterm and Omarska. Every day guards would walk around the camp, around the civilians, and call out some inmates. Those were usually eminent, either people with businesses of their own, businessmen, people who had money or who had a say of their own or who were in the police. Every day somebody would leave, some to Omarska to the camp, some to Keraterm and some went somewhere and we still do not know where they are. They never came back. One of them is my brother. My brother left and his son, they left to Prijedor. They never returned and they are still missing. My wife's brother lied next to me in the camp, and he was taken away. Branko Topola called him out, he was a bus driver, and he named General Zeric and Gutic. "One Gutic, come out." We thought they needed them to drive some buses or something, but they are still gone. Then six brothers, that is two brothers, two sons of two brothers, that is four and of their again cousins, two more sons, so two by two by two, six of them were taken away. Their name was Foric. They are still missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about in the camp itself, in Trnopolje camp, not Omarska or Keraterm, were there many interrogations that occurred there that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we were not really all interrogated. We were not all interrogated. There were people who were not interrogated, whereas in other camps, from what I have learned, they all had to be interrogated. No, that was not the case in Trnopolje. When I was detained there there were 19 of us, that is what we called, and we were more or less all beaten and battered and some could not even sit stone or lie down. Then a man came called Zika, I do not know him, and when he saw us, what we looked like, all beaten up, then he turned up all of a sudden at the door and asked them, all of them, "Why were you detained? Why were you interrogated?" When my turn came he asked me: "Why did they interrogate you? Did you have any arms?" I said: "I did have a pistol but it was for 10 or 15 years and it was quite a lawful weapon and I was a driver going out into the fields, so that I would have it with me because I drove goods, I never needed it." I said that I had turned over that pistol and he asked me if I had a paper to show that I had turned it over. I said, no, because nobody gave out any papers. I said I turned over my pistol to a soldier who was called Dej, that is what I learned by accident. He had here a mark, here somewhere on the chin. He said that I was telling the truth, yes, that there was such a soldier and that that was his name. He ordered another soldier, a Serb, to take me by the hand and he did too because I could not walk by myself. So they took me. There was a surgery nearby, an ambulanta in that same part, in the same compound, except that it was at the corner. He called a doctor, his name was Jusuf Pasic, a young man, a doctor. He threatened them and said: "You have got to help this man. Can you help him so that I don't have to take him to Prijedor now?" That doctor, the older one Pasic, replied that they could not really. He said: "We can give him an injection and tend to him here", but that some Serb minister or doctor or technician, somebody who was their boss and they know him too, he did not have one arm, that he did not allow that the inmates be taken to Prijedor to the hospital, but that they had to stay there and whatever happened to them. So I was given that injection and he told me: "Do you have any family members there, out there in the camp, in the school?" I said: "Yes, my sons." So he said: "Go, crouch into a corner and don't let these fools see you because they are fools and this madness will also pass." He patted me on the shoulder and said: "I am Zika and I know nothing." He stopped that interrogation. So then all those who were detained, taken into custody for interrogation, he let them go because all those who were interrogated were beaten up, were battered, were quite impotent. There were only a few lads behind who were not interrogated and they were not beaten either. So that that interrogation was stopped now. After that it would happen that they would take out someone, but it was much less and those perhaps were some private accounts that were being settled or they again looked for some, well, if somebody had perhaps some money or if he had had a conflict with somebody before, but there was no more systematic interrogation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see men taken out of the camp to perform work duty during the period of time you were in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a frequent occurrence. I remember ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am sorry. When these men were taken out, do you know whether they were bound in any way or were they under guard? Can you describe the circumstances how this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People taken out to work, no, they were not tied, yes, military went with them and guards, but they were not tied. They were taken with a certificate. The Camp Commander Kuruzovic issued them a piece of paper. Some would come back, but I remember when three left, they were under age, they went to load a truck with timber for a driver, a Serb, and one of the young men came back and he was all scratched because he was trying to escape and this one fired after him. They were Mahmuljin. Those two boys have never turned up. I would really like them to be still alive, but the mother of one of them came to the camp and cried and was asking to tell her where her son was, but nobody told them. Even the Camp Commander simply shrugged his shoulders and said: "I fear the worse." But I think he knew that they had been killed because they are still missing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of a night time do you recall whether or not girls were taken out of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was in the beginning, because in the beginning there were many women, girls, children. I believe over 20 convoys were formed from the Trnopolje camp for Banja Luka and then onward to Travnik and Bosnia, that free one controlled by the BH Army. In the beginning, as I told you, I was sleeping in the cinema and one night, it was a very turbulent night, soldiers came in with torch lamps and they were lighting the place and looking for something. We did not know what they were looking for, except that we saw the girls crying and begging them, "Not me, not me." But this did not help and many were taken out that night. If some of the men, the old ones, perhaps a father or a grandfather of a girl, would raise his head and say, "Don't take her, this is my daughter, my daughter-in-law" or whatever, he would be hit with a rifle butt or a kick. So that I heard a wail or a cry of pain of old men. I dared lift my head a little, but very cautiously. They were not close to me because this was a long hall, perhaps some 15, 20 metres, I would not know exactly, and I could see as they were moving where they would come closer, because that cinema was full of civilians lying down, of children and women and people. In the morning they would come back, but that night nobody slept, nobody could sleep. There were very many shots. If somebody would say something, then you could hear a Serb soldier cry out: "Well, throw a bomb, fuck your mother, throw a bomb and kill them all." I expected a bomb to fall amongst us, but nobody did throw a bomb. At any rate, the next day those girl that had been taken out returned. Somebody complained, whether it was the girls or parents or mother, somebody complained to the Commander, to Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the girls returned can you describe the state they were in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were terrified, terrified. They did not want to talk to anyone. We did not want to look at them because they felt embarrassed. They shied away from those around them. Whenever somebody would look at them they would look at the floor. They cried all day and they turned their faces to the wall because they felt ashamed. It was a disgrace. We who knew that, we also kept silent. We did not dare talk because we were also afraid. A day later soldiers came. I guess the Commander had criticised them. They came in a tank. There were very many soldiers on that tank with beards and with those caps and those markings, those Kokardas, and fired off, but they fired into the air, not at people. But they fired a lot and that is how they tried to intimidate us. They circled in the tank around the camp and we tried to escape. We tried to run for shelter in the school, somewhere not to be outside. Later on we learnt that that was the result of that night, that somebody had complained about the army, that the army was raping and things like that. So that they came there to scare us off, to intimidate us, so that we would not complain to the Commander again about such things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the average age of the girls that were taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew two by sight. They were perhaps around 22, 23, but believe me, I really felt embarrassed to talk to them. I only watched them, observed them, so that they would not know that I was observing them because I felt sorry for them. They were too embarrassed. They would not bear anyone looking at them. Mostly their age was 17, 18 or perhaps 30 if she was young and pretty and nice looking, she would also be taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, let me ask you regarding Exhibit 311A, B and C that you have submitted pursuant to Rule 70(C). I gather you have received the consent of the entity providing this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I think that is contained on the front of the letter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That says that it -- OK. You are saying that this letter gives you consent to publicise that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. Mr. Orie, you had said that you may have an objection as to accuracy. Perhaps I misheard you or misunderstood you. I was responding that you may have an objection as to authenticity. I gather what you are saying is that the maps here that are attached, these drawings, you may challenge their accuracy in terms of the placement of information on these maps, is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That, of course, could you challenge anyway by cross-examination, but they will be admitted. Depending upon what your challenge is we will then consider it. We will stand in recess until 2.30. (1.00 p.m.) (Luncheon Adjournment) (2.30 p.m.) PRIVATE

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, would you like to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think Mr. Orie wants to raise something.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to come back to the issue we discussed this morning of the documents that have been presented by the Prosecution. We have given it a better look than we gave Article 70, also a better look than we did before. The solution you suggested that would be suitable under these circumstances to challenge the accuracy in the cross-examination is, in our view, not finally an acceptable one.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, I meant to challenge the accuracy on cross-examination, not not to challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: I do not understand whether you have correctly understood.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What you have said to me to make me respond, I thought you said that my solution was to not challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: No, that is not what I meant to say at least.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to give some arguments for not accepting these documents as evidence. I think I had better do it now than when any witness might be confronted with these documents. If I understand well, these are drawings that are based upon what we expect to be satellite photographs taken, but that is not of major importance for us what the source is at this moment. If they would be put in evidence just as documents, then, of course, we could challenge at a later stage whether they are accurate or not and find our ways to do it. But when I do understand well, the Prosecution intends to use these documents to show them to witnesses and then, of course, the witnesses will reply upon questions that are dealing with this situation. First of all, we are still convinced and are even able, I think, to demonstrate that the documents are not accurate, so we are offering to at least convince you that these are not accurate documents. But, apart from that, and that might even be far more important, these documents contain a lot of information that may be highly suggestive if you show them to witnesses. For example, there are dates on it of what a situation at a certain place was, but not only dates, but also, for example, that there were buses there, that there was a crowd of people there, as I see on the map of 13th August 1992, and especially because we are so concerned about the accuracy because if the fixed buildings are not yet accurate, why would any indication of buses being on such a map, or crowds of people, be more accurate? Since we are highly restricted under Rule 70, especially (D) and (E), we are not in a position to call witnesses. You are even not in a position to summon witnesses on your own behalf, to tell us about how these documents were created, because this is an interpretation, I think, of photographs, several photographs -- I have no idea -- but if these documents are used to be given to witnesses, and if they see on these maps that at a certain date there were buses there or that there was a crowd of people somewhere, this is suggestive to a high extent. For that reason, we oppose strongly against accepting these documents as evidence at this moment. If you think it is necessary -- I do not know whether it is essential or not -- that we show that at least some inaccuracy is there, we are quite willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Your Honours, the Defence are saying that they are inaccurate, but in what way are they inaccurate? We have not heard one word as to that. I would be most interested to know how they say they are inaccurate, having regard to the date that these documents are said to have been created and having regard to what I understand of the Defence's access to the area. If they are inaccurate, then I think it is appropriate that we be told that so that some assessment can be made on the question of their admissibility, in particular, going to the question of whether or not they should be shown to witnesses. So, in the absence of hearing from the Defence as to how they are inaccurate, then I do not see how your Honours can be assisted in dealing with the question of admissibility. With respect to suggestability, then witnesses are giving their evidence of what they saw at the camp and what they experienced at the camp and are then shown the map or the plan. The witness can agree with it or disagree with it, say whether they recognise it or not recognise it. It is not a question of suggesting anything to the witness. It happens time and time again during the proceedings where a document that has been tendered in the course of proceedings by one witness or in some way is then subsequently shown to another witness. The witness deals with it as best the witness can. I cannot see how it suggests anything other than that. Most of these witnesses speak of the existence of buses. Most of these people speak of crowds of people being gathered around. I cannot see how it is suggestive. So, my submission, your Honour, without further from the Defence, I am not sure how one can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Can I ask you a question? Why do you think these will help us? We already have had sketch plans and innumerable photographs of Trnopolje. Nothing really turns on the geography very much, does it? My second question is, is it essential, from your point of view, to show these to witnesses? We have only two or three more left.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. It assists it ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: It just seems to me we are having a great debate about something that is probably of no great relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do not want to press this thing beyond what is necessary to press it, except that if a witness says that this appears to them to be a plan of Trnopolje camp, then that may be of assistance to your Honours. Very clearly, we have had a witness that has already drawn a plan. If one compares that plan with this plan, it may be sufficient. So I am not absolutely committed to the idea of showing it to a witness, except that I would have thought that it may have assisted your Honours in doing so. But it seems to me, your Honours, that this may be the only material that is available which purports to be a plan of the camp area at that time. Everything that your Honours have seen and had in relation to that is material that has been generated some considerable time after it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: One final question: the interpretation of "crowd of people and buses", is that essential for your purposes? If that were removed, would it reduce the value of these, from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If that is the basis upon which the Defence are objecting to it, and if they can explain why that, having regard to the evidence that has already been tendered through the witnesses, is a difficulty, then that is a matter that we will take under consideration, your Honours, in an effort to resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What are your concerns with respect to this Exhibit? Let us see if we can put it in the proper framework. You are offering this under Rule 70(C) which provides that, "If the Prosecutor is in possession of information which has been provided to him on a confidential basis and which has been used solely for the purpose of generating new evidence, that initial information and its origin shall not be disclosed by the Prosecutor without the consent of the person or entity providing the initial information and shall in any event not be given in evidence without prior disclosure to the accused". Before we recessed, I wanted to make sure that there had been this consent and that is what Mr. Niemann says this covering letter of 311 says, that when it said that they may be used in court proceedings, that is sufficient consent to reveal the identity of the source, etc. or at least the source in so far as the identity of the country providing this information. (D), I understand there are concerns, but I think that the Rule contemplated that a document like this would be offered by the entity that provides this information. So that we would not just have a document that comes into evidence, but that whoever provided this information would then be the witness and it would come in through the witness. Then, of course, the Rule goes on to provide for cross-examination but that limits you in your cross-examination. So I suppose the problem is that when this piece of paper just, kind of, comes in by reference to a witness who has not prepared this document, it is hard to challenge it because he has not prepared it. He does not know whether it is accurate or not, but if he is given the document where there are suggestions about what exists that he might be more prone to say, "Oh, yes", nod his head, "it says 'a crowd of persons', therefore, it must be a crowd of persons". But I would follow with Mr. Niemann's concern and that is, Mr. Orie, what is there about any of these three plots or diagrams that you contend is inaccurate? Let us see if, perhaps, we can deal with that and there may not be a problem, as I think Judge Stephen is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ORIE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the problem is not, perhaps, the inaccuracies we found only but, of course, first of all, the Prosecutor is claiming that this is the only material that relates to the situation in August 1992. First of all, we are not in a position to verify whether this is true or not because we cannot hear any witness, so that is a claim already. If there are minor inaccuracies which we can more or less demonstrate now, of course, we have no possibility to demonstrate whether it is inaccurate as far as the buses and the crowds of people are concerned, but if it is inaccurate in certain points, then, of course, you will understand that we fear that it might be inaccurate on the other issues as well. I must say that part of it, if you are just talking about buildings, then it is of lesser concern to the Defence although, as a matter of principle, I think it should not be allowed because it is apart from fixed buildings, there are also tents on it, etc. etc., and I do not see how this material is necessary for a witness to testify on the situation he has found at that moment. If you would like to have an indication of what is inaccurate, if I may draw your attention, it is the same on all three drawings, that there is a rectangular building just at the junction of the road, just north of it, and just south of what we have been told was the shed where building materials were sold. In our view, that is not a correct representation of what must have existed at that time there. There was an electrical -- there was a building on a different place and a different shape. Apart from that, I noticed that although the drawings are very precise as showing even shelters, that one of the fixed buildings, one of the Prosecution's witnesses has told us about, it was a toilet building just south of the dom building, is not represented on these drawings. I would like to make a final remark on one of the arguments that has been used by the Prosecutor. He said, "Well, witnesses have been presented pictures and photographs and other witnesses had told already about that". As far as I remember, there was an order of your Court that the witnesses should not speak to each other and not get any information on what happened during the earlier Court hearings. So, that is not an argument that convinces me highly, but these are just two things. There are a few more, but especially these two, toilet building, the witnesses have stated, the Prosecution witnesses have said, it was there. We have pictures of that. It is still there. So, of course, it may be possible that they just have been removed for 13th August, but that does not seem very likely to me. The electricity building is, quite clearly, not in the position and not in the shape as we find it on our photos. If you would look at these photos, you would see that these buildings have been there for a very long time. I am quite willing to show them to you. We have not prepared any copies.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Orie, your objection will be granted. The documents, you do not have a challenge to the authenticity. Your concern is with accuracy. Whoever prepared this is not here for you to cross-examine. It appears to me that if they came in and then offered to the witness, the witness, of course, could argue against this exhibit and challenge the exhibit, but it would be suggestive, certainly for lay people. If you took off, for example, the "crowd of people", that would help. What is troublesome, though, is that it really does not provide any information to the Chamber that we do not already have. We have an Exhibit 309, Prosecutor's Exhibit 309. That was a drawing that was prepared by one of the witnesses of Trnopolje camp. We have had a lot of testimony. We have had at least two videos, as I can recall, of Trnopolje camp, several, several photographs. My personal concern is that the party preparing this document is not here for you to cross-examine, and that any inaccuracies that may exist in this document cannot really be developed in the way that they should be. So it would not really help us. So, therefore, your objection will be granted. Exhibit 311 will be removed from evidence -- Exhibit 311A, B and C. Mr. Niemann, would you call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are continuing. MR. ENIZ BESIC, recalled Examined by MR. NIEMANN, continued

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, do you know the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have known him for some 10 years before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the circumstances of how it is that you came to know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I knew his father better. He was a serious man. He took part in that war back then, since its early days and he was a man who was well respected in Kozarac. Dule Tadic I met when he was already grown up and when he began engaging in this karate training, and he also was a coach for my son for about a year, my middle son. I advised my son to give up the course because he had kidney complaints, so that my son quit. That is how I met Dule Tadic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your son learning from the accused Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Why, he was learning, he was training, he was practising karate. This, what is it called, karate trainings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where Dule Tadic lived in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it in Kozarac, where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That part in the centre of Kozarac and it belongs more to Krkici. It is right next to Kozarac, as you get off the Banja Luka/Prijedor road above a restaurant to the right, that is where Dule Tadic's house was and he had a coffee bar. As I was a driver, I often went to Mrakovica by truck and I saw him often, and I also often times would walk past his house in day time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the times you knew him before the war, do you know whether he had a beard or was he clean shaven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he had beard more often than not. Not really a long one, but I have known him longer with beard than without a beard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were in the Trnopolje camp, did you ever see Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the first time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately after a month of my stay in the camp, perhaps a few days more. I do not remember the date because I really did not think about dates. I was wondering whether I would survive. Once I saw him next to the -- across the school in the on the road as he was talking to a guard. I did not see him enter the grounds. He was standing and talking to Serb guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it day time when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was day time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how far were you from him when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me see, it was 15, maybe 20 metres. I was in front of the school and he was on the road. The school is not far away from the main road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say this was about a month after you arrived, so it is likely to have been sometime in June 1992, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could have been end of June, perhaps the early days of July, somewhere there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a military uniform, multi-coloured military uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the predominant colour in this uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, they had several kinds of uniform, and they would turn up in different types of uniform. I mean, all the Serb guards and soldiers. There was a multi-coloured uniform, military one, and then there was a police uniform which was blue and there was also a police civilian blue, but it was slightly multi-coloured, a little camouflage, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able now to remember whether it was the police camouflage uniform or the military camouflage uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not the police uniform, I mean, the blue one, the real blue civilian police uniform. It was more a military, of many colours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he armed on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and there was an automatic rifle on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing when you saw him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Standing on the road, and there were several guards gathered around him, around him and they talked. They were together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise anyone he was standing with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I may have, at the time I did not have time because by the time I saw him I turned, as I already had some early experience. If you saw anyone you knew, what we called a neighbour, then it might cost you your life or, at least, a beating. So, even as I recognised -- even had I recognised anyone, I would have turned back to the school where one's place was because I would be afraid, although I had nothing, no conflict with him before the war, but I did not -- I felt uneasy. I was slightly afraid. I have had that experience, that neighbours or friends were killed by their neighbours or friends or beaten up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him was he clean shaven or did he have a beard on the first occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had a beard, a short one, yes, he had a beard then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second time you saw him, when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was perhaps a week later, whether he was in passing or had he come on some business but, in any event, he turned up some seven or 10 days later. He appeared again on that same road, not with those same guards, but he was again in the company of guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come into the camp at any stage when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see him enter the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him on the second occasion where were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since I lived in this school, in the so-called library, I would go out either to go to the toilet or to prepare some food. Since I was preparing some food, there were several of us, and we prepared our food together because there was no organised kitchen or anything. There was a joint cauldron. It could feed some 300, 400 people and we were not less than 1600, so that not even 30 per cent of people could eat there. That meant that one had to fend for himself, and I would have to go out, but if there they would be somebody on the road as I went out, I would get out of that sight -- of their sight and I avoided to go out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw him from outside of the school building and he was on the road when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How was he dressed on this second occasion when you saw him, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in civilian clothes at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was armed with a pistol then. I did not see the rifle, but they are all very brief scenes so there is not much looking around. I mean, the moment I saw it was Dule Tadic, I rather moved away than stand there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just finally about the camp, were there toilets located outside of the buildings and out in the open in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since that was a school it had its toilets inside, but since the water supply was cut off, they were all blocked, there was no water for use and they were locked also, so that we had to go outside to relieve ourselves, outside the school. At first, some holes were dug out and those, you know, those wooden pallets were put over them, and then they were surrounded with blocks, with elements of about a metre, a metre and a half, so that as one went there to relieve oneself, his head stuck above that fence. It was really filthy and whenever it rained they would overflow and it all floated, all this filth, all that just floated around the school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it dangerous at times to use the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, both by day and by night. At night it was slightly less dangerous if it was really dark. If it was a quiet night, it was also dangerous to be seen by a guard because they tended to fire. In day time, one had to walk very warily and sometimes they would fire, and you had to go back, you could not go to the toilet and then wait for an hour or even more to try again. It depended on the guard. Some tried to provoke more and fired more, some less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people using the toilets from time to time fired upon by the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, especially if a man, if an inmate took a bottle with water because there was no toilet paper -- sanitary conditions were very bad and one would take a bottle with water to wash himself -- and then they would fire and you had to discard the bottle, and you could hear the voice swearing "Balija mother" or using offensive language against something Muslim, so that you had to discard that vessel with water, if you had one, and go back, and then try either to hide if you could hide that container with water or just not take along it because it was dangerous to take water into the WC.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where did the guards fire upon the prisoners using the toilets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They fired from a post below. There was a road from Prijedor to Trnopolje, and there was a post which was quite good. They had good visibility because they were a little away from the school -- a little bit away from the school, and they could see people well and then provoke people who went there to relieve themselves. I remember that post, where it was on the road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there a number of guard posts around the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were very many guards and very many sentry posts, points, as they called them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These sentry points that were located around the camp, were they used to guard the camp or were they used to guard the roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only to guard the camp, so that the inmates would not leave the camp or escape. But sometimes they also used those guards to control those who might move along, and it applied to civilians, that is, women who brought food for their husbands or sons, and those guards controlled what they brought, that is, those bags and whatever was in those bags, and such like. But their principal responsibility was that an inmate who had come out of the -- that the inmates do not leave the camp, because all the machine guns, all the rifles, were aimed at the -- were turned towards the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, would you please look around the courtroom and tell me if you see the person you know and recognise as Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: --- please point to that person, describe where he is sitting in the courtroom and the clothes that he has on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dule Tadic is sitting to my left. He is wearing a dark blue suit, a tie, clean shaven, sitting in the middle between two policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Might the record reflect, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no more questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss de Bertodano, cross-examination? MISS DE BERTODANO: Yes, your Honour. Cross-examined by MISS DE BERTODANO

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, you were not a friend of Dusko Tadic's, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not someone whose house you would visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or who you would have a drink with or socialise with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him in Kozarac you saw him in passing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By and large, in passing, sometimes in the company of some other Kozarac people with whom he would be talking, since I often went past his house practically every day, and sometimes even several times a day, so that I could see him often when I passed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, can you remember when the last time you would have seen him would have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall, but I used to see him in Kozarac until the war itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us today about two occasions on which you saw him while you were in Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Today you have been telling us about two occasions on which you saw him while you were staying at Trnopolje camp, that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the first occasion you have said that it was a month or possibly more after you arrived at the camp, so late June, early July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot be more specific about a date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I mean, dates were not the things that were on my mind and I was not interested in Dule, and there were words, so that I never wrote down or remembered the dates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw him you were coming out of the school building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was outside, yes, I was outside the school building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw him on the road talking to a group of guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember which way he was facing, whether he was facing towards the school building or towards the road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all around, he was looking all around. He was talking to people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember how many people were in that group of guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Three or four guards, I would not know exactly, but they were around him and they were talking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cannot help us with the names of any of these guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know, I spent four months there. Very, very many guards had -- passed through the camp, and I really could not be sure who were the guards then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Also you told us that you did not have time to see who the other guards were or to recognise the other guards because you knew that when you recognised people that could lead to bad experiences, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so, maybe it would not have but I was afraid because of the previous experience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have told us that Dusko Tadic was wearing a camouflage uniform, but you cannot assist us in any detail as to what the colours of the camouflage uniform were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I can do. That was a camouflage uniform, a multi-coloured, military, camouflage uniform. Just a moment, a camouflage uniform, the military one, and the police camouflage uniforms, they are quite alike, but the police uniform is slightly darker and more blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were some 15 to 20 metres away from this scene at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then told the Court that you saw him a week later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was in more or less the same position as you had seen him the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, he was on the road with a group of guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember who any of the guards he was with were on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the Court that both these scenes were very brief scenes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, long enough to recognise him and to go back, to get away from his sight, back to the room where I used to spend time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you first asked to recall these scenes to anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question was when you were first asked to remember these scenes, these two scenes, that you have told us about today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was -- it was some interrogator, somebody who asked questions, some investigator who came to me whom I gave an interview, who paid me a visit and I gave him an interview about everything, not really about everything. There was not time for that because I could go on for days and nights. This is only a small fragment, one per cent of it. So that I was found, asked to give an interview and I agreed. I do not remember. There was somebody with an interpreter whom I did not know, but not -- that person is not present here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would that have been in about January of this year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. It was winter time. I think it was January. MISS DE BERTODANO: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Redirect, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Besic being permanently excused? MISS DE BERTODANO: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Besic, you are permanently excused. You may leave. Thank you for coming. You are free to leave. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Miss Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have prepared the motion that we discussed this morning ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: --- the oral motion that we have made. We have prepared the written motion. We will provide a copy to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Are we going to hear from witness No. 73 now?

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, it will be Samir Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will look at the motion. You may call Mr. Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We will call Mr. Samir Hodzic. MR. SAMIR HODZIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, would you please take that oath that is being given to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated. Examined by MISS HOLLIS

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Samir Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 10th October 1970.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you born in a hamlet about one and one half kilometres from the village of Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be provided Prosecution Exhibit 305, please? Mr. Hodzic, if you could look at this map and take a moment to orient yourself, please? If this map could be placed on the overhead projector, please? Could you please take the pointer that is on the desk there by you, and if you could point us to your house, where it was located near the village of Trnopolje? So this is the house that is located just to the left of the intersection below the word "Trnjani"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend primary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you attend secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Maribor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you completed secondary school in Slovenia, did you remain in Slovenia and take technical training there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What training did you receive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became a metal worker, I graduated from school which allowed me to work as a metal worker.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you lived in Slovenia, how often did you visit your home in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, once a month perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you called up to do your compulsory military service in 1991 while you were living in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you first serve in Stip, Macedonia, and then in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were your duties in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was with the artillery. I was a site -- I was calculating the targets, siting targets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you leave the JNA in December of 1991 before your compulsory service was completed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you leave the JNA before completing your service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I could not stay there any more. I could not endure it any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to your home in Trnopolje in December 1991 and live with your family there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you live at home until 9th July 1992 when you were taken to a camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you lived in Trnopolje as you grew up there and then after you came back from the service, how often would you visit Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I went two or three times a week, Saturdays and Sundays were regularly, always.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why would you go to Kozarac several times a week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply for amusement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you go there for any reasons other than entertainment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I needed something, when I had to do some shopping in some of the shops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Kozarac where would you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mostly frequented coffee bars and such like, some restaurants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the main business street in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, so .....

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Dule Tadic first pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometime at a time when I came out of the primary school.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall how many years it would have been before 1992 that he was first pointed out to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four or five perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you know about Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew he was an instructor or trainer of karate in Kozarac and afterwards that he was the owner of one of the cafes in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This cafe in Kozarac that he owned, did you ever go to this cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How often did you go there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I went Saturdays and Sundays when I would go both Saturday and Sunday to Kozarac, and sometimes I would be there, sometimes I would go only on Saturday, sometimes only on Sundays, but more or less I went there often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The times that you went to Dule Tadic's cafe, was he ever there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I would not see him every time. Sometimes I would see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of that cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was called "Nipon".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where else would you see Dule Tadic besides his cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I used to see him in the street and I once saw him in front of a restaurant which was called "Nejra" and so in the street and such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever socialise with Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the time that you knew Dule Tadic to see him, did you ever see him with facial hair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, sometimes he had a beard, sometimes not. It depended on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the attack on Kozarac, do you recall when you last saw Dule Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe seven days, maybe 10 days, before the outbreak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, at this time I would like you to look around the courtroom and see if Dule Tadic from Kozarac is in the courtroom. If so, I would ask you to point to him and tell us what he is wearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman is sitting between the two policemen. He is dressed in a blue jacket and blue shirt and he has a multi-coloured tie. As far as I could see, he has bags under his eyes.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note a correct identification of the accused.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, the record will reflect that the witness identified the accused.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, on 9th July what were you doing before you were taken from your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was doing some farming work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was working with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My father was with me, my uncle and another neighbour whose mother was a Serb and father. We used to call these people Ukrainians, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your father's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esef.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your uncle's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Munib.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that Munib Hodzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, 9th July, were you made to join a column of men moving in the direction of the Trnopolje detention camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else from your home had to join that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Myself and my father and from our house, myself and my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your uncle also join the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you, your father and your uncle moved along in the column, were other Muslim men forced to join the column as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Zuhdija Turkanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Simply he was my neighbour, some 150 to 200 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, what is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zuhdija Turkanovic also taken in the column with you on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the men escorting the column wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the men escorting the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the way to Trnopolje camp, was your uncle Munib called from the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After he was called out of the column, what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard him being -- one of the soldiers that were standing in front of the house called him out and he stepped outside of the column.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since my uncle that day had a hat on his head, the one who called him out, he said, "You in the hat, come on over here", and he simply got out of the column and I heard him say, "What do you need?" so .....

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that what did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After some 10 metres, as we kept on moving, I could hear a spray, a round of fire from an automatic weapon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see your uncle Munib Hodzic again after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you moved along the road in the direction of the Trnopolje camp, did you join with another column of men from Elezovici and Matrici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your arrival at Trnopolje camp, were you put on buses and then taken first to Omarska and then on to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why you were sent on from Omarska to Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that there was no room for us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long were you held in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From July 9th to, I believe it was, 20th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Keraterm where were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In room -- the last room of that building. They were called -- room No. 4 it was called.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Hakija Elezovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at Keraterm camp did you see Hakija Elezovic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken after Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Upon your arrival at Omarska, what happened to you and the other detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were beaten as we were walking to the perimeter of the camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you made to assume any particular position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were lined in a column against a wall and we were facing the wall and leaning with our hands, that is, with three fingers against the wall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With your hands in the Serbian three finger position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were made to assume that position, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To my right, there was a man who was writing names and birth dates and father's name and, as he was writing the names down, there were three soldiers behind him and they were beating him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were beating the man writing the names down or they were beating the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With what were you being beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With feet, hands, batons, rifles -- whatever they wanted to use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they seem to concentrate their blows on any particular parts of your body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What parts of your body were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Since we were facing the wall, those were blows to the back, to the spine or the kidney area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were beaten, after you had to lean up against the wall and were beaten, where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the building which we called the white house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What room in the white house were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the smallest room which was as you walk into the white house not -- neither left nor right but straight ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a small room at the end of the corridor as you went into the white house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If could I have this photograph marked as Prosecution Exhibit 312 for identification? The colour photograph and three black and white copies. Would you please show that to the Defence? They have been provided a black and white copy. If that could be provided to the witness, please? Mr. Hodzic, do you recognise the room depicted on that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What room is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is that room, the little one that I mentioned just now, the room that is straight at the end of that hallway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that photograph could be placed on the overhead projector, please? Your Honour, I would offer Prosecution Exhibit 312 for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Exhibit 312 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MISS HOLLIS
utterances.text: Mr. Hodzic, how many people were put in that room when you arrived at Omarska that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All 27 of us that were transferred that day from Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How crowded was that room with all of you in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was so that we could barely squeeze inside, simply we were just packed one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What were the conditions like in that room while you were in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The conditions were bad -- you can say horrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The windows in the room, were the windows opened or closed for you while you were in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the most part it was all closed. The window, the little window that you see in the photograph up there, they opened for us, in my opinion, only if they were satisfied with something, when they, sort of, showed mercy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Hakija Elezovic in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Zuhdija Turkanovic in that room with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you held in that end room until the day you were taken for interrogation?
